articles.title: Tata boardroom feud is testing a trusted business empire
articles.summary: The dispute raises questions about the Indian conglomerate's governance, succession plans and future.
articles.body:
Before dawn breaks over Mumbai, Mansi Kadam begins preparing vada pav, a savoury snack synonymous with the western Indian city, for the day's customers. One ingredient is non-negotiable: Tata salt.

When asked whether she would ever consider switching brands, her reply is a reminder of an old Hindi ad jingle, "If it's salt, it has to be Tata."

She knows little about the developments unfolding in the boardroom of the Tata group, one of India's oldest and most influential business empires that makes everything from salt to software.

But her instinctive loyalty points to a question confronting the group: Can one of India's most trusted brands remain insulated from a public battle over power, governance and control?

A recent public disagreement between the board of Tata Sons, the holding company of the Tata group and Tata Trusts, its principal shareholder, has put a spotlight on the conglomerate.

At the centre of the dispute are two issues - the proposed public listing of Tata Sons and the reappointment of chairman N Chandrasekaran . Most of the Tata Sons board, including its biggest minority shareholder SP Group, supported the decisions.

But Noel Tata, chairman of majority shareholder Tata Trusts, has opposed both resolutions. He maintains that a public listing would dilute the group's philanthropic ethos and is likely to get both decisions overturned at its annual general meeting.

"When we say this is a governance crisis, it's a misalignment of interests between the board [of Tata Sons] and the shareholders [Tata Trusts]," Shriram Subramanian, head of independent corporate governance firm InGovern Research, told the BBC.

While he does not expect the brand's image to be affected immediately, he flags concerns over the leadership's ability to navigate the challenges.

Disagreements within the Tata Group have been simmering since the death of former chairman Ratan Tata - Noel Tata's half-brother who designated him successor after his death - in 2024. For many Indians, Ratan Tata's philanthropy and leadership had become inseparable from the brand. His death triggered widespread mourning and experts say it left a leadership void in the group's image with the public.

The Tata group has topped India's most valuable brand list by valuation consultancy Brand Finance since 2018, according to the group's website.

Tata Sons, the business entity, is described by the group as the "fastener keeping the many disparate elements of the whole together".

Tata Trusts, which represents seven philanthropic trusts that own the majority stake in the group, is widely regarded as its moral compass, guiding the businesses on social impact and philanthropy.

For many Indians, both the entities together make up what most companies cannot buy - trust.

Now with these entities in rival corners, that is coming under strain.

"Once upon a time, there was a unified audience which said the Tatas are good people with good governance. Today, the opinion is divided," said Harish Bijoor, business and brand strategy consultant.

While most consumers appear unfazed, the dispute has polarised other stakeholders including business partners, investors and employees. Some view it as corporate power politics, others as a genuine governance debate, but few agree on which side is right, Bijoor said.

"This conflict has brought the Tatas into conversations everywhere, which is not good as they have always liked to be out of it," he says.

The group has traditionally preferred being low profile about philanthropy and conflict resolution.

The Tata group did not respond to BBC's email with detailed questions.

Founded by Jamsetji Tata in 1868, the Tata group expanded under JRD Tata who transformed it into a professionally managed conglomerate. Ratan Tata drove its global ambitions through acquisitions.

Tata group, which has a combined market value of more than $260bn (£195.6bn) and employs hundreds of thousands of people in more than 100 countries, is not new to controversies.

The conglomerate has faced protests over industrial projects, scrutiny of its Indian telecom business during a spectrum allocation controversy, a high-profile dispute with Japan's Docomo and, more recently, questions over Air India's performance .

Some of its business decisions have also drawn attention, particularly Tata Steel's troubled Corus acquisition, though other overseas bets such as Tetley and Jaguar Land Rover were successful and helped expand the group's global footprint.

Its biggest controversy was in 2016 when the Tata Sons board abruptly removed Cyrus Mistry as chairman and brought back Ratan Tata as interim head. Mistry, heir to the SP Group, was chosen by a team led by Ratan Tata himself. It led to a long battle which ended in 2021 with the Supreme Court ruling in the Tatas' favour.

Last month, journalist Sucheta Dalal wrote in her column for Moneylife magazine that the Tata group has "weathered serious governance storms" and enjoys "special privileges available to no other business group [referring to a tax exemption granted to Tata Trusts for holding shares in Tata Sons]" because of a reputation built over decades.

In an email interview, Morgen Witzel, a fellow at Exeter Centre of Leadership who wrote a book on the brand in 2010, cited several examples on the group's connection with people.

At Jamshedpur in Jharkhand state, where the group set up India's first integrated steel plant and an industrial city, it provides healthcare and education to people in hundreds of villages. Watchmaker Titan supports employees who want to leave and start their own businesses. Tata Motors at Pune has supported thousands of female entrepreneurs, he points out.

"It is the concatenation of all of these things that builds trust because people see that, by and large, Tata is there to serve their needs rather than just take their money," Witzel said.

But while the group has weathered other storms, this time, the divide is within.

The boardroom tussle has increasingly spilled into the public domain, with Tata Sons and Trusts clashing through legal notices and conflicting statements.

Venu Srinivasan, vice-chairman of Tata Trusts and a nominee director on Tata Sons' board, has sought a probe into alleged governance lapses at some trusts. The trusts deny the lapses.

Noel Tata has made two proposals to avoid listing the company.

First, that the Tata Sons board buy back a portion of SP Group's minority stake as a "fair and equitable solution" to the latter's demand to monetise their stake. Secondly, restructure Tata Sons by merging with itself two businesses which would change the way it is classified by India's central bank, helping the group potentially avoid a listing.

It is not clear whether he can pull this off, given that unlike Rata Tata, he had not consolidated power yet.

"Ratan Tata's larger-than-life image is, to some extent, the reason behind the current conflict. Everyone was deferential towards him and his successor was known only after his death through his will," says Subramanian.

Had Ratan Tata overseen the succession himself, the transition would have been smoother, he says.

Brand expert Bijoor calls for the Tata group to put together a "white paper" on how the conflict plays out in the end. "They stood for transparency, and they must never shed that."

How the influential group manages these tensions may offer a glimpse into its future. The outcome will be watched closely across corporate India, where Tata's governance and business practices have long been regarded as a benchmark.

articles.title: Publicly owned rail is popular. But is it making the trains run on time?
articles.summary: Meeting travellers' expectations could be challenging, experts warn.
articles.body:
The early afternoon of Wednesday 6 August was an unremarkable one on the rail network. Then suddenly, shortly before 14:00, a power failure brought trains across the north-west of England to a halt.

Chaos ensued: passengers told the BBC they were stranded on platforms for hours, with some having to book hotels for the night.

This incident, stemming from a short power cut that affected Network Rail's operating centre in Manchester, was, in itself, unusual. But it added to a difficult summer for train passengers.

Repeated heatwaves required risk control measures like speed reductions to avoid tracks being damaged in the heat, leading to delays and cancellations. There was a serious derailment near Lewes, East Sussex, and another smaller-scale incident near Wickford in Essex soon after.

Against a backdrop of relatively high cancellation rates and steep fares compared with previous decades, rail users could be forgiven for forming the impression that things are not working.

Something is changing, though: Labour is steadily bringing nearly all passenger rail services into public hands. Nationalisation is a popular idea - a YouGov tracker poll suggests almost two thirds of the public support public ownership.

But in reality, plans are still in their early stages. Big structural changes have yet to be introduced. And experts caution that it's too early to say how successful these will be.

So can rail nationalisation meet the public's expectations? Or are the ongoing delays and cancellations that we're currently seeing under a part-nationalised network a sign that it might struggle to deliver real improvement?

South Western Railway (SWR) was nationalised in May 2025, the first of six services to be brought into public ownership under Labour so far.

At Woking station, which is served by SWR, regular commuter Leo tells me he had been optimistic about public ownership, but hasn't noticed it making any difference so far: "I think the phrase 'emperor's new clothes' comes to mind… it's still unreliable."

SWR saw a clear increase in cancellations during its first year in public hands.

But how much of this was due to nationalisation?

The Conservatives have cited SWR as an example of how public control does not necessarily mean improvements or fix key problems.

But the government argues SWR's early period in public hands was affected by high summer temperatures, signal failures and trespass incidents.

Lord Hendy, the rail minister, says work to turn the operator around has included introducing long-delayed new trains on suburban routes and recruiting more drivers, resulting in a drop in those cancellations that are due to staff shortages.

TransPennine Express was nationalised in May 2023, under the Conservative government. Many passengers had been at their wits' end as the operator struggled to fulfil its timetable and suffered from poor industrial relations.

A plan to improve reliability was put in place, which included cutting some services and even removing one type of train as a way of sorting out staffing problems. A new deal with the drivers' union also helped - something an insider at the former private sector operator claimed to me their company had not been permitted to do.

So has it worked? Cancellations have fallen noticeably. But they were still above the Great Britain average in the year to August.

It's really important to say the data can only tell us so much. There are so many different factors that might affect the performance of each service: for example, the state of the infrastructure it relies on, weather events or simply how well it was working before the government took over.

Plus, of the operators nationalised since Labour came to power, only SWR and c2c have completed a whole year in public hands. Even for those nationalised years earlier, the picture is clouded by the impact of the pandemic, when passenger numbers fell off a cliff.

But according to Alex Hynes, chief executive of DfT Operator Limited (DfTO), the government company that currently owns publicly-run operators, it has been possible to make some short-term changes. Notably, these include making one team jointly responsible for managing infrastructure and passenger train services in some areas including the south-west of England.

"The railway is a system: track, train, people," he says. "So by putting one person in charge, they can fix all elements of the system to deliver a better service to customers."

Hynes also gives examples of changes on the recently nationalised Thameslink; investment in better cleaning, improving toilets and replacing unpopular upright "ironing-board" seats.

But when it comes to the pure performance data of operators nationalised in the past few years - delays, cancellations - can we really draw any conclusions yet to tell us whether the policy is working?

"I think it's completely hopeless to try and do that assessment over such a short period," Stephen Glaister, a former chair of regulator the Office of Rail and Road who is now emeritus professor of transport and infrastructure at Imperial College London. He thinks a decade is needed to assess the impact of nationalisation.

The government argues that official data suggests publicly owned train operators are performing better on punctuality and cancellations overall than those still under DfT contracts to private operators.

Experts point out that whoever is running the passenger trains, some limitations remain. Many delays happen because infrastructure, like signals, fails. There's only so much capacity on the existing network. And getting better trains or more staff can take years.

The view that privatisation ultimately failed, leaving unreliable services and high fares, may be widespread. However, Prof Glaister argues that for a few years in the 1990s, the old privatised system actually worked well. Operating costs and subsidies were falling while the number of train services and passengers went up, he says.

And in the current context, it's important to be clear about what nationalisation really means.

The railways Labour inherited weren't, in truth, completely privatised, and nationalisation doesn't mean a return to British Rail.

For example, the infrastructure manager Network Rail has been fully under public control for over two decades. A number of train companies including LNER and Northern had already been nationalised under the Conservatives. Scotrail, Transport for Wales and Caledonian Sleeper are controlled by devolved national governments.

And even those operators still on contracts issued by the DfT at Westminster have been heavily controlled by the government for years. During Covid, private operators started being paid a fixed fee to run services, while the taxpayer took on the financial risk. The terms of the contracts meant train companies had to "ask government for permission to blow their nose", according to one senior industry executive, who asked not to be named so they could speak freely.

Highly profitable rolling stock companies ("ROSCOS") still own the actual trains. Freight companies operate privately too, and there are a handful of fully commercial "open access operators" on the rails like Lumo, Hull Trains and Grand Central - although there are concerns within the industry that these could end up squeezed.

So what is often referred to as the nationalisation of the railways, in fact amounts to gradually returning passenger train operators run by private companies to public hands as their contracts expire - and making this the default.

What will Great British Railways do differently?

This is not all that's happening, though. The government hopes that re-organising the railways under a new publicly run body, Great British Railways (GBR), will make a big difference. This will bring together the running of trains and tracks, ending the current fragmented system.

A botched rail timetable introduction in 2018 was the spark for the then-Conservative government to eventually propose GBR as a new overarching body - although the Tories believe private competition should not be excluded from the system.

Some trains are already covered in distinctive GBR branding, but the organisation still doesn't exist. A new law to create it is making its way through parliament. Unknowns remain, like exactly how GBR will interact with devolved governments, and who its senior leaders will be.

Transport expert and author Prof Jon Shaw, of the University of Plymouth, says the idea of a "single guiding mind" should create "a better planned railway that's more aligned to the customer".

Prof Shaw thinks potential benefits include better long-term planning around rolling-stock and timetables, and the removal of "the compensation merry-go-round", where train companies and Network Rail argue about whose fault a delay was.

Hynes says: "The way you get the railway to work is you get the infrastructure and the trains and the people working in harmony because it's a system. And we can do that in a publicly owned GBR railway in a way that we haven't been able to do for a generation."

But Prof Shaw cautions of potential pitfalls. For example, "there remains very little money", and "a massive issue is whether or not the rail minister or DfT more generally - or the Treasury - will be able to butt out" and leave rail leaders to run the railway.

Prof Glaister also fears politically sensitive aspects such as fares and levels of service could lead to politicians trying to run the railways themselves, because of the amount of public money involved.

"Actually, governments are not very good at running railways," he says. "So you want management who are somewhat independent and able to run it."

Lord Hendy insists that despite the Transport Secretary having ultimate sign-off on GBR's strategy, the body will be genuinely arms-length from government.

"The point of this is to get a cadre of people who are committed to the outcomes that the secretary of state and I want for it, who can go off and run it on their own," he says, adding: "They'll have a lot more chance in the future than they've had in the last 20 years."

The railways are currently subsidised to the tune of around £12bn a year - not including spending on major projects like HS2.

The Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander says that she wants to see subsidy levels fall. Meanwhile, Network Rail has acknowledged a squeezed budget means difficult choices, and shoring up the network against the effects of more extreme weather requires investment.

Prof Glaister says: "When the public is hoping for a better level of service, more reliability, fewer breakdowns and lower fares, what they're really asking for is more money to be put into the railway.

"I don't think it's likely the government is going to be able to find more money, probably [it will have] less, actually. And so I think there's a real problem with ministers raising expectations from this policy."

But Hynes doesn't see a contradiction between reducing taxpayer subsidy and making train services better.

"My two north stars are performance up and subsidy down," he says. "If the service is better, we get more customers, we get more revenue."

Lord Hendy and Hynes also push back on the idea that the answer to improving reliability might be running fewer trains.

Hynes says: "In an industry with high fixed costs, the best way of getting the subsidy down is to go for growth."

Questions also remain about how GBR will manage industrial relations. Terms and conditions currently vary across operators. What will cost-conscious ministers do if unions seek to standardise these at the most generous level across the network?

While ministers argue they are getting on with improvements that people will notice, there's acknowledgement that the speed of improvement will vary between operators.

Lord Hendy says some changes "ought to be dead boring… to make sure tomorrow is a little better than today if you can do it".

But he says "more than 30 years worth of behaviors" will need altering to make the railway run solely in the interests of the customer.

At Woking, is there optimism that things will improve in the long run?

"I really hope so," says Leo, "it would be amazing - as it's not the best service now."

articles.standfirst: Suspeito é um homem de 54 anos, que foi preso em flagrante após primo da vítima buscar ajuda. Crianças aprenderam sobre o sinal após verem sobre ele na televisão e terem uma conversa sobre o assunto com a avó.
articles.summary: Suspeito de 54 anos foi preso em flagrante após primo da vítima buscar ajuda. Crianças aprenderam sobre o sinal após verem sobre ele na televisão e terem uma conversa com a avó.
articles.body:
Uma menina de 9 anos foi salva de uma tentativa de estupro depois que fez o sinal universal de pedido de socorro, na manhã de sexta-feira (9), no bairro Sítio Cercado, em Curitiba .

Segundo a Guarda Municipal, o suspeito é um homem de 54 anos, que foi preso em flagrante por tentativa de estupro de vulnerável.

A menina estava indo para a escola, acompanhada de outras crianças – entre elas o primo de 10 anos – quando foi abordada pelo homem. Ele ofereceu dinheiro para que ela o acompanhasse, mas ela recusou. Em seguida, o homem segurou com força a mão da menina e começou a conduzi-la.

Com medo, a única reação que a criança teve foi fazer o sinal de socorro, que consiste em dobrar o polegar para dentro da palma da mão e fechar os outros quatro dedos sobre ele.

O primo dela viu o sinal, correu e procurou ajuda em um posto de combustíveis. "Eu cheguei falando que o homem estava tentando roubar a minha prima. Eles já levaram a sério", lembra o menino.

Câmeras de segurança registraram parte da movimentação. Nas imagens, é possível ver o momento em que o menino corre até o posto para pedir ajuda. Logo depois, aparecem a prima dele e o suspeito. Outra câmera mostra o menino pedindo ajuda aos funcionários e clientes do posto. Alguns deles vão em direção ao homem, pedindo que ele fique no local, mas ele sai correndo.

Os frentistas acionaram então uma viatura da Guarda Municipal que passava pela região e o homem foi preso em flagrante por tentativa de estupro de vulnerável.

Segundo a Guarda Municipal, ele já era monitorado por tornozeleira eletrônica desde 2017 por estupro de vulnerável.

Criança aprendeu a fazer o sinal após ver na TV

Criança faz sinal universal de pedido de socorro e homem é preso por tentativa de estupro de vulnerável, em Curitiba — Foto: RPC

Em entrevista à RPC, a menina e o primo contaram que aprenderam sobre o significado do sinal depois que viram reportagens na televisão e conversaram com a avó sobre o assunto.

"Eu sabia [do sinal] pela TV e pela avó ensinar. Ela falou que, quando nós estivermos em perigo, é só fazer o sinal que daí as pessoas ajudam", detalha a menina.

Segundo a avó, ela sempre busca conversar com as crianças sobre medidas de segurança que elas devem tomar, especialmente quando estão longe de adultos conhecidos.

"Eu sempre ensino para eles, para que, quando eles saírem na rua, eles prestem atenção, nunca fiquem muito perto das pessoas, não conversem com estranhos, não aceitem doce, dinheiro... Na televisão também sempre aparece aquele sinal para pedir socorro. Eu passei isso para eles também. Quando passava na televisão, eu falava: 'Isso serve para vocês também. Qualquer perigo que você estiver, assim que puder pedir ajuda, faz assim com a mão. Quem conhecer esse sinal vai saber que vocês estão precisando de ajuda'", detalha a avó.

O primo, que ajudou a salvar a menina, conta que, assim que recebeu a orientação da avó, já levou a sério e guardou a informação.

"Eu olhei, daí eu aprendi, e não levei na brincadeira", afirma o menino.

Sinal de socorro usado por mulheres em situação de perigo — Foto: g1 PR

O sinal universal de socorro foi criado no Canadá. Uma agência de publicidade de Toronto desenvolveu, em abril de 2020, uma campanha com ações para conter o crescimento dos casos de violência doméstica registrados no período de confinamento da Covid-19. O intuito era criar um gesto simples e seguro que poderia ser utilizado por vítimas de violência doméstica para denúncias, sem que o agressor percebesse o pedido de socorro.

Segundo especialistas, ao perceber alguém fazendo o gesto, a orientação é tentar se aproximar da pessoa de forma discreta e amigável, como se conhecesse a vítima, e levá-la para um local seguro, como um comércio ou uma farmácia.

A recomendação é conversar com a vítima e encaminhá-la aos órgãos competentes, como a delegacia.

Se não for possível se aproximar, a orientação é procurar a polícia e relatar a situação.

articles.title: Caso Gisele: Tenente-coronel acusa peritas de armação para incriminá-lo, mas laudos e imagens da polícia contestam sua versão | G1
articles.standfirst: Geraldo Neto afirma que Gisele Alves cometeu suicídio, mas perícia aponta inconsistências em sua versão. Imagens de câmeras policiais também contradizem parte do relato. Nesta semana, ele passou por seu último interrogatório antes da justiça decidir se ele irá a júri popular.
articles.summary: Geraldo Neto afirma que Gisele Alves cometeu suicídio, mas perícia aponta inconsistências em sua versão. Imagens de câmeras policiais também contradizem parte do relato. Nesta semana, ele passou por seu último interrogatório antes da justiça decidir se ele irá a júri popular.
articles.body:
O tenente-coronel Geraldo Neto, acusado de matar a esposa, a soldado Gisele Alves, afirmou ser vítima de uma armação durante seu último interrogatório antes de a Justiça decidir se ele será levado a júri popular. Em imagens exclusivas exibidas pelo Fantástico deste domingo (11), o oficial contestou a reprodução simulada do crime e acusou as peritas de terem remontado uma árvore de Natal para incriminá-lo.

“As peritas foram, remontaram a árvore, demoraram ali quase 10 minutos pra remontar a árvore. Só pra me acusar”, afirmou Neto durante o depoimento. Segundo ele, na manhã da morte de Gisele, havia terminado o relacionamento e estava tomando banho quando ouviu um barulho forte. Ao sair do banheiro, diz ter encontrado a esposa caída na sala.

O laudo da reprodução simulada contesta essa afirmação e indica que uma árvore de Natal encobria a visão dele.

Além disso, imagens das câmeras corporais dos policiais militares que atenderam à ocorrência registraram a árvore intacta na sala. Um bombeiro que participou do socorro também confirmou a posição do objeto.

A defesa do tenente-coronel Geraldo Neto pediu à Justiça que ele responda ao processo em liberdade. Mas o oficial segue preso preventivamente. O Ministério Público é contra a soltura e alerta que, em liberdade, o tenente-coronel pode usar sua influência para comprometer o julgamento.

Neto reagiu ao pedido de liberdade feito por seu advogado juntando as mãos em gesto de oração.

A defesa de Geraldo Neto se manifestou por meio de nota e afirmou que confia na impronúncia, ou seja, que o tenente-coronel não será levado a júri popular.

Geraldo Neto faz sinal de oração enquanto seu advogado fala — Foto: Reprodução/Fantástico

"Eu acho que é um caso de repercussão emblemático e que diga para a sociedade um basta. A mulher não pode mais continuar sendo vítima de machismo e de feminicídio como está ocorrendo no nosso país", encerra o advogado José Miguel Júnior.

articles.title: SP começa a multar quem desrespeitar regras para bicicletas e patinetes elétricos nesta terça-feira | G1
articles.standfirst: Multa é de R$ 130 e será vinculada ao CPF do infrator. Regras para circulação estão em vigor desde agosto e estabelecem limites de velocidade e locais permitidos para bikes e patinetes.
articles.summary: Multa é de R$ 130 e será vinculada ao CPF do infrator. Regras para circulação estão em vigor desde agosto e estabelecem limites de velocidade e locais permitidos para bikes e patinetes.
articles.body:
A fiscalização das regras para a circulação de bicicletas e patinetes elétricos na cidade de São Paulo começa nesta terça-feira (13). As normas estão em vigor desde agosto e preveem multa de R$ 130, vinculada ao CPF do infrator.

Os agentes da Companhia de Engenharia de Tráfego (CET) serão responsáveis por constatar as infrações, com apoio da Guarda Civil Metropolitana (GCM). Entre os pontos fiscalizados está a circulação de bicicletas e patinetes elétricos em calçadas exclusivas para pedestres.

Em um dia de feriado, por exemplo, a Avenida Paulista fica com menos carros e mais bicicletas, patinetes e pessoas praticando corrida.

Nesta segunda-feira (12), quem aproveitou a folga para se exercitar encontrou banners com alertas sobre os limites de velocidade. Agentes da CET também distribuíram panfletos e deram orientações aos frequentadores.

No dia a dia, porém, o desrespeito às regras de circulação é registrado em diferentes pontos da cidade. Na ciclofaixa da Avenida Tancredo Neves, por exemplo, foi flagrado um veículo autopropelido com placa circulando na faixa exclusiva para motos. Já na Avenida Brigadeiro Tobias, no Centro, um condutor invadiu a faixa de ônibus.

Patinetes elétricos compartilhados na cidade de São Paulo. — Foto: Reprodução

O contador Francisco das Chagas avalia que o respeito às regras ainda não é suficiente, principalmente nos locais com maior movimento. Para ele, a convivência no trânsito também depende do respeito aos pedestres e aos demais usuários das vias.

“Respeito ao pedestre, né? Sempre parar no semáforo para o pedestre atravessar. Ele que tem a prioridade. Tem que ter em mente o respeito e não fazer com o outro o que não gostaria que fizesse com você”, afirmou.

A bióloga Mônica Batista considera importante a fiscalização para organizar a circulação de bicicletas e patinetes elétricos. “Já tem umas pessoas sinalizando na hora da gente parar, na hora de passar na faixa”, disse Mônica.

O servidor público Fernando Vasconcelos também avalia que quem segue as normas não precisa temer a fiscalização. “Acho que, andando de acordo com a regra, não tem do que ter medo”, afirmou.

Veja as regras para bicicletas e patinetes elétricos em São Paulo

Patinete elétrico na Avenida Engenheiro Luís Carlos Berrini, em São Paulo — Foto: Marcelo Brandt/g1

As normas estabelecem limites de velocidade e definem os locais onde bicicletas e patinetes elétricos podem circular. As regras variam conforme a sinalização e as características da via.

Nas ciclovias e ciclofaixas, bicicletas e patinetes elétricos podem circular a uma velocidade máxima de 20 km/h. A circulação de pedestres nesses espaços não é permitida.

Quando a ciclofaixa fica em uma calçada e o espaço é compartilhado com pedestres, as bicicletas devem circular a, no máximo, 6 km/h. Nesse caso, os patinetes elétricos não podem circular pelo local.

A mesma restrição vale para os canteiros centrais em que bicicletas e pedestres dividem o espaço: patinetes elétricos não podem circular nessas áreas.

Nas vias sem ciclovias ou ciclofaixas, bicicletas e patinetes elétricos podem circular em ruas com limite de velocidade de até 50 km/h. Os condutores devem seguir pelo canto da pista, no mesmo sentido dos carros.

Os patinetes elétricos também podem circular em vias com velocidade máxima permitida de até 40 km/h, desde que o próprio equipamento não ultrapasse 20 km/h. Já as bicicletas comuns e elétricas são proibidas em vias de trânsito rápido e rodovias sem acostamento.

A publicitária Andreza Alves considera que a organização dos espaços depende também da consciência dos usuários.

“Eu acho que é bem organizado. Eu acho que é mais uma questão de consciência mesmo. Aqui é um local que é para bicicleta, é para bike. Se a gente está parando aqui, a gente está correndo o risco”, disse.

articles.title: NPR CEO who previously called First Amendment a 'challenge' to receive 'First Amendment Award'
articles.summary: NPR CEO Katherine Maher will receive Harper's Magazine First Amendment Award despite once calling the amendment a "challenge" to fighting disinformation.
articles.body: NPR CEO Katherine Maher will receive Harper's Magazine's "First Amendment Award" later this month despite her past criticism of the amendment. "As president and CEO of NPR, Katherine Maher has guided one of America’s most important public media institutions through a period of extraordinary political, legal, and financial scrutiny, reaffirming journalism’s essential role in a democratic society," the magazine said in a press release earlier this year about Maher receiving the James C. Goodale First Amendment Award on Oct. 26. Harper's Magazine also claimed that Maher led NPR "through a period of heightened scrutiny and challenge" along with "successfully battling" President Donald Trump's efforts to defund NPR, though Congress still rescinded $1.1 billion in federal funding to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting in 2025. NPR GETS $80 MILLION GIFT FROM DEMOCRATIC MEGADONOR IN MAJOR BOOST AFTER LOSING GOVERNMENT FUNDING Although the magazine hailed Maher as an advocate for journalism, Maher has not always been supportive of the First Amendment as a whole. In 2021, when Maher was the CEO of Wikimedia, which oversees Wikipedia, she discussed efforts to combat disinformation and considered the First Amendment a "challenge" in that goal. "The number one challenge here that we see is, of course, the First Amendment in the United States. [It] is a fairly robust protection of rights and that is a protection of rights both for platforms, which I actually think is very important that platforms have those rights to be able to regulate what kind of content they want on their sites," Maher said. BILL MAHER TELLS NPR INTERVIEWER HE VIEWS OUTLET AS 'FAR EXTREME OF THE LEFT' She added, "But it also means that it is a little bit tricky to really address some of the real challenges of where does bad information come from, and sort of the influence peddlers who have made a real market economy around it." NPR has also had a history of questionable journalism. Most notably, NPR declined to cover the Hunter Biden laptop story in 2020 ahead of the presidential election in what many critics saw as an effort to protect then-presidential candidate Joe Biden. Maher, who was not appointed NPR CEO until 2024, later conceded that the publication "made a mistake." NPR OFFERING STAFF BUYOUTS AFTER RECEIVING $113 MILLION IN CHARITABLE GIFTS "I do want to say that NPR acknowledges we were mistaken in failing to cover the Hunter Biden laptop story more aggressively and sooner," Maher said during congressional testimony in 2025. Fox News Digital reached out to Harper's Magazine for comment. Tim Graham, executive editor of the media watchdog NewsBusters, told Fox News Digital, "Harper's Magazine is demonstrating the usual liberal impulse, that being fiercely critical of Trump and the Republicans is what the First Amendment is all about. But NPR didn't hold President Biden accountable. Instead, they insisted that covering corruption in Biden's family was a 'distraction.'""Their explanation for this pride is that Maher courageously fought off defunding NPR, which, of course, is not true. They are defunded. Liberals believe depriving NPR of taxpayer subsidies is some sort of First Amendment violation. But it's not a First Amendment violation for NPR to avoid having any Trump-supporting conservatives on their airwaves to push back on all their liberal bias," he continued."These people have no shame that Maher championed aggressive censorship of ‘bad information,’ just as European socialist countries have done. Maher said in a 2021 TED Talk that the First Amendment was a ‘challenge,’ a hurdle, something that makes censorship ‘a little bit trickier.’ How does that deserve a First Amendment award??" he asked. NPR celebrated Maher receiving the award, pointing to its past statement when reached for a comment by Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Public media exists to serve the public interest, and I can think of no greater service to the public than the defense of the First Amendment," Maher said in a comment. "The freedom, imagination, and initiative of all Americans flourish with its protections, so that we may better understand the world and one another. The compact of citizenship asks that we each step up to defend our constitutional rights if they are threatened. On behalf of NPR and the NPR Network, I am deeply honored to accept this award."

articles.title: Online marketplace jewelry listing tied to armed robbery in affluent Tennessee city
articles.summary: A Facebook Marketplace jewelry listing lured armed robbers to a Franklin, Tennessee, home, sparking a police chase and three arrests on felony charges.
articles.body: A Facebook Marketplace jewelry listing was linked to a late-night armed robbery at a home in affluent Franklin, Tennessee, where police pursued three fleeing suspects, authorities said. Officers responded to a home in northeast Franklin just after 11 p.m. Friday, Oct. 9, and determined the robbery was connected to jewelry advertised for sale on the platform, according to the Franklin Police Department. The suspects fled the area but were spotted by responding officers a short time later. A vehicle pursuit followed, ending with all three men in custody, police said. FLORIDA MEN INDICTED IN ARMED HOME INVASION WHERE SUSPECT POSED AS UTILITY WORKER, 13-YEAR-OLD ZIP-TIED: DOJ Authorities identified the suspects as Ivan Lagos-Espinoza, 22, and Jose Paiz-Godoy, 23, both of Nashville, and Rubel Rodriguez-Lisa, 19, of Lebanon. All three face multiple charges, including aggravated robbery, felony evading and tampering with evidence. The robbery unfolded in a community known for its wealth and high-end homes. Franklin’s city website describes it as "one of the wealthiest cities in one of the wealthiest counties in the United States." Franklin's median home sale price reached $903,410 in September 2026, while the median listing price stood at $1.1 million, according to Realtor.com. Across Williamson County, where Franklin is located, the median home sale price was $929,990, the real estate website reported. 119,000 FAKE SHOPS COULD STEAL YOUR CREDIT CARD DETAILS Police credited the Williamson County Sheriff’s Office with helping investigate the robbery and apprehend the suspects. The case also prompted a warning to online sellers about the risks of bringing strangers to their homes, particularly when expensive merchandise is involved. Police urged buyers and sellers to arrange exchanges in public, well-lit locations with other people nearby and surveillance cameras whenever possible. For valuable items, authorities recommended meeting at a police department or another law enforcement facility. WASHINGTON JEWELRY STORE OWNER OPENS FIRE AFTER WOULD-BE THIEVES RAM TRUCK THROUGH STOREFRONT Sellers should also bring someone along, avoid carrying large amounts of cash and limit the personal information they share, including details about their homes, schedules and other valuables, police said. Authorities warned that jewelry, electronics and other expensive items can make sellers attractive targets for criminals. "If something about the buyer, seller or proposed meeting location does not feel right, cancel the transaction," the department advised. articles.title: ABC accuses FCC of trying to 'inflict maximal coercive pressure' with probe against network
articles.summary: Disney's latest filing accused the FCC on Monday of using early broadcast license renewals to dodge judicial review and exert coercive pressure on ABC.
articles.body: Disney and ABC accused the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) on Monday of using the license renewal process to circumvent "judicial review" and inflict "maximal coercive pressure" against the network and company. Disney originally sued the FCC in August over what it claimed was a "retaliatory campaign against ABC" regarding the agency's early broadcast license renewal proceedings for eight ABC-owned stations earlier this year. The stations, according to the FCC, must demonstrate they are operating in the public interest as the agency investigates diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) practices. However, in Disney's latest filing, the company asserted that the FCC could have used "a number of different tools" to investigate Disney and ABC's DEI practices that did not involve forcing stations to renew their licenses years ahead of schedule, suggesting it was done to avoid legal scrutiny. ABC MORE CAUTIOUS OF BOOKING CANDIDATES ON 'THE VIEW' AMID FCC PRESSURE, DISNEY'S FIRST AMENDMENT LAWSUIT SAYS "These are not merely 'theoretical' tools ... they have been used by the agency for decades," the filing read. "Yet the agency tried none of those less intrusive tools here, instead taking the unprecedented step of calling for early license renewal of all eight ABC-owned stations at once. Defendants’ own admissions leave no doubt as to why — Defendants sought to inflict maximal coercive pressure on the media company whose speech the Administration sought to curb, while deliberately evading judicial review." Disney cited a court hearing last week in which the FCC was instructed to provide a supplemental filing on alternative methods the agency could have used. During the hearing, the FCC suggested that additional procedures would have required federal court enforcement. "That Defendants openly describe judicial review as an obstacle demonstrates what Plaintiffs have been saying all along: shielding their unconstitutional campaign against ABC from judicial review is part of Defendants’ retaliatory strategy," the filing read. In a comment to Fox News Digital, FCC spokesperson Adam Jackman dismissed the latest filing as an effort to block the FCC in court procedures. CONSERVATIVE GROUPS URGE FCC TO BACK OFF ABC LICENSE REVIEW, WARNING IT COULD HURT RIGHT-LEANING MEDIA "Disney’s latest filing only confirms that they’ve filed a meritless case in the wrong court at the wrong time," Jackman said. "They want a district court to prevent the FCC from even considering whether Disney has complied with its longstanding obligations as a broadcaster. The law does not allow that. The FCC will continue to hold broadcasters accountable to their regulatory obligations." Fox News Digital also reached out to ABC and Disney for comment but did not immediately receive a response. Disney and ABC have repeatedly attacked the FCC's probes and investigations into the company as a form of retaliation over programs and hosts that are critical of President Donald Trump, such as late-night host Jimmy Kimmel. DISNEY ACCUSES TRUMP'S FCC OF ATTEMPTING TO 'SUPPRESS SPEECH' WITH LICENSE RENEWAL INVESTIGATION CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In addition to the license renewal proceedings, the FCC has launched a probe into the ABC daytime talk show "The View" based on the agency's demand that broadcast stations adhere to the equal opportunity requirement stating opposing political candidates receive equal time. Disney has maintained that "The View" is a "bona fide news" program exempted from the rule.

articles.title: Hundreds more prisoners to be freed in second phase of early release scheme
articles.summary: Second tranche of prisoners will include those serving up to two and a half years for crimes.
articles.body:
About 650 more offenders will leave jails in England and Wales early on Tuesday in the second phase of the government's plan to tackle the prison population crisis.

The group will include offenders serving up to two and a half years for crimes.

Under the new rules, they are leaving jail after serving a third of their sentence behind bars, rather than half.

The second wave of releases comes as the government takes its plan to radically overhaul criminal courts back to Parliament - but also as probation officers prepare to vote in a ballot that could lead to a strike over pay and workload.

Some 700 offenders left jail early on 1 October - all of whom were serving terms of less than 19 months.

Tuesday's second stage begins the process of releasing batches of offenders serving increasingly long sentences - culminating next June with those serving more than 12 years.

Napo, the probation service union, said the releases have put enormous strain on its members, who are charged with monitoring the offenders in the community.

Typically, those being released should expect to be electronically tagged and subject to other monitoring conditions for the second third of their sentence.

On Tuesday, the union's members will meet to discuss next week's vote, which could lead to strike action. Probation officers have been offered a 5% pay rise by the Ministry of Justice (MoJ), while it had demanded 12% as part of a plan to make up for loss of earnings caused by cuts from 2010.

The MoJ says the offer is fair and has been accepted by two other unions and is twinned with a £700m investment in probation to recruit 1,300 extra officers and the roll-out of AI tools to cut the workload of monitoring offenders.

While the second phase of prison releases gets under way, the government is bringing its criminal court reform plan back before MPs, after announcing a week ago that it had abandoned the most controversial element of it.

The revised plan drops proposals for a new form of Crown Court where a judge alone, sitting without a jury of ordinary people, would reach a verdict against suspects facing up to three years in prison.

However, jury trials will still be scrapped for the most complex and long fraud cases - and another 5,500 trials will be kept in the lower magistrates court by ending a defendant's right to ask for a jury trial.

The government says it will expand the use of so-called "blitz" or "short trial" courts after pilots have shown that grouping similar cases together can speed up their progression through the courts - cutting backlogs.

One of the pilots at the Old Bailey led to the London backlog of 500 cases concerning assaults on emergency workers being cut in half over the summer.

A major review of criminal courts by former appeal judge Sir Brian Leveson recommended more virtual hearings for defendants to slash wasted time bringing them to and from cells. The government has now ordered pilots for defendants to appear direct from police cells.

On Monday, the government announced it had accepted more than 150 of his 180 recommendations to modernise the criminal courts.

It has rejected his advice to retain a restriction on volunteer magistrates that means they can only jail an offender for 12 months. Under the government's plan magistrates will have the power to jail for up to two years - the aim being to keep more cases out of Crown Court, to help clear backlogs.

articles.title: Ethiopia’s Tigray war: Where do the UAE and Saudi Arabia stand?
articles.summary: The Tigray conflict puts the UAE’s backing of Ethiopia and Saudi Arabia’s diplomatic role under scrutiny.
articles.body:
Addis Ababa, Ethiopia – As renewed fighting in Ethiopia’s Tigray region threatens to destabilise the Horn of Africa, public backing by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) of Ethiopia’s federal government and Saudi Arabia’s record of regional diplomacy are drawing scrutiny.

Both Gulf powers have strategic interests in the Horn of Africa, but their roles differ. The UAE has publicly backed Ethiopia’s government while Saudi Arabia has previously helped broker an Ethiopia-Eritrea rapprochement and was reported to have offered to mediate between the two countries in 2025.

The renewed fighting threatens to unravel the November 2022 Pretoria peace agreement, which ended a war between Ethiopia’s federal government and Tigrayan forces. As tensions with Eritrea add to the risks of a wider confrontation, the positions of Abu Dhabi and Riyadh offer a window into the interests of external powers in the crisis.

The UAE: Clear alignment, unproven leverage

On September 25, the UAE condemned attacks by the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and its allied armed groups against Ethiopian federal forces, the seizure of airports in Tigray and the escalation in the neighbouring regions of Afar and Amhara.

Sheikh Shakhboot bin Nahyan Al Nahyan, the UAE minister of state, expressed solidarity with Ethiopia’s government and people, reaffirmed support for the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and called for an end to hostilities, the protection of civilians and adherence to the Pretoria Agreement.

The statement made Abu Dhabi’s public position clear: It backs Ethiopia’s federal government while calling for de-escalation and dialogue. It did not establish whether the UAE was providing military assistance or had secured commitments from the parties to end the fighting.

The UAE also has commercial interests across the Horn of Africa. Dubai Ports World (DP World) operates Berbera port in Somaliland, and a shipping route launched in 2025 connects the port with Jebel Ali in the UAE, providing an additional corridor for cargo serving inland destinations, such as Ethiopia. Landlocked since Eritrea’s independence in 1993, Ethiopia relies heavily on Djibouti for access to international trade.

These commercial links help explain Abu Dhabi’s interest in regional stability and its relationship with Addis Ababa. However, they do not establish that the UAE can influence the TPLF, persuade Eritrea to de-escalate or change Ethiopia’s military calculations.

The extent to which Abu Dhabi can use its relationship with the federal government to encourage a political response to the conflict remains unclear.

Saudi Arabia: Diplomatic experience, uncertain engagement

Saudi Arabia has yet to publicly announce its position on the latest fighting in Tigray.

The kingdom has not publicly commented on the renewed war, according to an October 1 analysis by Critical Threats, although it undertook diplomatic efforts earlier this year to reduce tensions between Ethiopia’s federal government and the TPLF.

Saudi Arabia has previously sought to mediate between Ethiopia and Eritrea. In November 2025, Chatham House reported that sources said Riyadh had offered to mediate between the two countries amid rising tensions over maritime access and regional security.

A June 2026 analysis by Germany’s SWP think tank said previous Saudi mediation efforts had failed, partly because negotiations did not address Ethiopia’s interest in the Eritrean port of Assab.

The kingdom’s broader regional alignment also matters. An August 2026 analysis by the Soufan Center described Saudi Arabia and Egypt as backing Eritrea in opposition to Ethiopia’s ambitions for Red Sea access.

This is an assessment of regional alignment, however, not evidence that Saudi Arabia is directly providing military support to Eritrea or the TPLF in the current fighting.

Saudi Arabia has a strong interest in Red Sea security, a vital corridor for international shipping and its own oil exports. Whether Riyadh will take a more public diplomatic role as tensions escalate remains unclear.

Egypt’s rivalry with Ethiopia adds to regional tensions

Egypt’s role in the crisis is shaped by its longstanding dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) and its growing ties with Eritrea.

Cairo has also stressed that responsibility for the governance and security of the Red Sea rests with countries bordering the waterway, a position shared by Asmara. The issue has added to regional tensions as Ethiopia seeks reliable access to the sea.

In September, Ethiopia’s army chief, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula, accused Egypt and Sudan of supporting armed groups fighting the federal government, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF).

His remarks, reported by Al Jazeera on September 28, did not provide evidence substantiating the accusation. Egypt’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Nader Zaki, subsequently reaffirmed Cairo’s commitment to state sovereignty and non-interference, rejecting suggestions that it had departed from those principles.

He did not directly address the specific allegation of Egyptian support for the TPLF.

Egypt’s relationship with Eritrea has nevertheless become an important part of the regional picture. President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi met Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki in Cairo on June 8, 2026.

According to Egypt’s presidency, the talks covered bilateral cooperation, developments in the Horn of Africa and Red Sea security.

The two leaders also stressed the importance of coordination to maintain regional stability. The meeting highlighted closer cooperation between Cairo and Asmara, but did not establish that either country was involved in the renewed fighting in Tigray.

For Cairo, the dispute with Ethiopia extends beyond Tigray to the Nile and the balance of power in the Horn of Africa.

Its relations with Eritrea and its disagreements with Addis Ababa form part of the wider regional context, but they are not evidence of direct Egyptian involvement in the renewed conflict. Whether these regional relationships will affect the course of the fighting remains uncertain.

The risks extend beyond Tigray. Ethiopia’s pursuit of maritime access has become a source of tension with Eritrea, whose Red Sea coastline includes the port of Assab. Addis Ababa argues that reliable access to the sea is a national priority while Asmara rejects any threat to its sovereignty.

Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of sending troops across the border and supporting armed groups. Eritrea denies the allegations and has called on the United Nations Security Council to intervene. The allegations remain contested, but deteriorating relations have raised the stakes of renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia.

A wider confrontation could put more civilians at risk, complicate humanitarian access and disrupt regional trade and security. It would also test whether external partners could encourage restraint without appearing to endorse either side’s military objectives.

The UAE’s close ties with Addis Ababa could provide a channel for diplomatic engagement while Saudi Arabia’s record of regional diplomacy offers a possible opening for renewed talks. However, the available public evidence does not establish that either country is currently leading an initiative to contain the crisis.

The UAE and Saudi Arabia should not be cast as pursuing opposing strategies simply because one has publicly backed Ethiopia’s federal government while the other’s current position is less visible. Their interests and diplomatic approaches differ, but the evidence does not show that either has decisive influence over the fighting.

Their contribution should be assessed by whether they can help secure concrete steps towards de-escalation, renewed political dialogue and a reduction in tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Public statements, commercial interests and past diplomatic achievements may create opportunities for engagement, but they are not substitutes for progress on the ground.

The Pretoria Agreement remains the framework for a political settlement in Tigray, yet renewed fighting underscores the difficulty of sustaining peace while underlying disputes persist. A durable settlement will depend primarily on the parties themselves. External partners could contribute by encouraging restraint and supporting credible negotiations.

For now, the UAE’s public alignment with Ethiopia and Saudi Arabia’s diplomatic record offer different potential channels for engagement. Whether either country can turn those relationships into a meaningful contribution towards de-escalation remains unresolved.

articles.title: UK growth forecast upgraded but energy prices and rates to bite in 2027
articles.summary: The IMF report comes as final preparations are being made to the first Budget under Prime Minister Andy Burham.
articles.body:
The UK economy is forecast to grow by more than previously expected this year before higher energy prices and interest rates hit growth in 2027, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has said.

The organisation's latest report, which is closely watched by the government, said the UK economy would expand by 1.3% in 2026, up from the 1% it predicted in July, before slowing in 2027.

Economies across the world have proved more resilient to the energy price shock caused by the US-Iran war, the IMF said, but it warned the economic fallout from the conflict remained "highly uncertain".

Chancellor John Healey said the government would look to "provide some breathing space" for households in the Budget.

Healey is making the final preparations to Andy Burnham's new-look government's tax and spending plans, which will be announced on 28 October.

Government borrowing costs have surged, placing pressure on the chancellor to ensure his plans are credible in the eyes of financial markets, which the UK relies on to borrow money.

But IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro told BBC News on Tuesday that the UK's process of managing its debts is now leading the major G7 economies.

"As you know, the UK has already started the consolidation process and it is the country that basically stands out, along with India", she said.

The organisation said the UK is one of the only major economies on course to stabilise levels of national debt. It projects the UK will reduce its annual borrowing by nearly four percentage points of GDP from 2025 to 2031, significantly more than the rest of the G7, many of which are increasing their deficit over this time period.

The UK is also projected to have the lowest annual borrowing in the G7 in 2031, and the longest maturity of debt, locking in lower rates for longer.

Asked if the UK was one of the countries the IMF was telling to reduce borrowing, Tenreyro said that the country had begun the process already and should "stay the course".

The head of the IMF has previously called on the world's advanced economies to cut borrowing and reduce debt levels.

The reversal of downgrades to economic forecasts made at the start of the US-Iran war, mean the UK is expected to have the second-fastest growing economy in the G7 along with Germany.

But growth is estimated to slow in 2027 to 1.2% due to higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weighing on household spending and business investment.

Healey acknowledged that wars in the Middle East and Europe were "hitting people in the UK and around the world", but added that "Britain's economy is showing strong international resilience".

When the economy is growing, businesses tend to invest more, more jobs are created and people, on average, tend to feel better off. The opposite can occur if the economy stagnates or shrinks.

Maike Currie, head of personal finance for Pension Bee, told the BBC the IMF's report "does give the chancellor a little bit of breathing space" but that "it doesn't mean that families are feeling better off just yet and I don't think it is a gamechanger".

On Tuesday, the Resolution Foundation called on the chancellor to make "make repairs" to the public finances, but said well-targeted support was needed for those "struggling to heat their homes".

"The challenge of continuing to bring down borrowing must be paired with the pressing need for fresh cost of living support to help families facing a difficult winter ahead," the think tank said.

Andrew Griffith, Conservative shadow chancellor, said if Healey "reaches for more tax rises" in his Budget, "he is choosing slower growth and working people will pay for it".

Burnham has pledged to create "good growth in every postcode" as part of his plans to giving nations and regions more control, but his strategy has faced criticism inside his own party.

The IMF said households are likely to continue feeling the pinch of rising prices, with inflation expected to average 3.3% this year and remain above the Bank of England's 2% target in 2027 at 2.8%.

The Bank itself has predicted inflation could rise above 4% at the beginning of next year - making it more likely that interest rates will rise.

Healey is expected to meet with other finance ministers at the IMF's annual meeting in Bangkok, Thailand, on Tuesday to discuss how the economic impact of the Middle East and European conflicts could be limited.

The IMF said the global economy had shown a "remarkable capacity to absorb shocks" not just from the current Middle East conflict, but also from the Covid pandemic and Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title: Afghanistan SAS inquiry: Investigator says team prevented from following evidence
articles.summary: Military police investigator tells an inquiry that the probe into suspected murders was "dictated" from above.
articles.body:
A military police investigator has criticised a murder probe into alleged SAS executions, claiming senior officers prevented his team from following the evidence.

Delme Williams, who investigated allegations against one SAS unit, told a public inquiry: "It was not a standard investigation where investigators were making decisions based on where the evidence led them."

He added that he remained convinced members of British special forces should have been criminally charged.

It is the first time the inquiry, which is examining allegations the SAS committed murders in Afghanistan that were covered up, has heard from those involved in military police investigations into special forces operations.

Williams, who served as deputy senior investigating officer for Operation Northmoor which looked at 11 SAS operations, told the inquiry on Monday that the course of the investigation was being "dictated" to his team from above.

He added that he questioned whether the senior Royal Military Police officer in charge, known as the Gold commander, was being "influenced to close the investigation".

Williams recalled an occasion during Operation Northmoor when investigators were discussing photographs of one of the 11 SAS operations they were investigating for suspected murder.

The operation involved the fatal shooting of nine people at a home in Nad Ali district, Helmand Province, in February 2011. The youngest person killed was aged 14.

Williams told the inquiry that, based on his experience as a seasoned crime-scene investigator, he wanted to show the images to a forensics expert.

Operation Northmoor investigators suspected those shot had been killed unlawfully, and the photographs showed bullet marks low to the ground, which appeared to undermine the SAS account that those killed had been standing and fired at British forces first, before the SAS returned fire.

Williams told the public inquiry: "A picture paints a thousand words - photos are ideal evidence."

The military police officer said he was "quickly shut down in an abrupt matter" by the Gold commander and when he tried to push back, his senior officer pulled rank and it would have been "insubordinate" to go any further.

He said he believed, to this day, the photographs should have examined by an expert.

BBC Panorama investigated the same incident and travelled to Helmand to visit the site of the shooting.

An RMP investigator confirmed to the BBC that they had seen photographs from the scene and that the bullet mark patterns had raised alarm among the Operation Northmoor team.

"You can see why we were concerned," the investigator said. "Bullet marks on the walls so low to the ground appeared to undermine the special forces' version of events."

Panorama's team examined what appeared to be bullet holes from the raid, still visible, which were clustered together on the walls low to the ground.

The BBC showed photographs from the scene to forensics and ballistics experts, who said that the clusters suggested multiple rounds had been fired downward from above, and did not appear indicative of a firefight.

This supported the version of events put forward by bereaved family members of some of those who were killed. Those relatives have told the BBC those killed were all unarmed civilians who were shot in their beds, and that appears to corroborate the RMP investigators' suspicions.

At the time, the Ministry of Defence said the incidents had been subjected to "extensive and independent investigation" by the RMP, and no prosecutions had resulted.

Operation Northmoor, set up by the RMP's serious crime team, was investigating 45 killings by an SAS squadron in 2011 during a single tour of Afghanistan.

The military police officer told the inquiry the investigation team thought the operational photographs could be important evidence and were looked at "in quite some detail", and the dismissal of this evidence was an example of the way in which the investigation was being run.

Williams told the inquiry there were "outside forces" that seemed to him to be directing the course of the investigation.

"I do recall a general feeling that inquiries were being stopped too soon and that there was no appetite... to pursue all lines of inquiry or for anyone to be referred for prosecution."

The BBC reported in 2022 evidence from another Operation Northmoor investigator, who told Panorama: "I believe there was pressure from above to shut down the investigation. It became increasingly clear to me that it didn't matter what evidence we were able to gather, these cases were never going to be allowed to go to court."

During the course of his sworn testimony, Williams was shown a number of internal military documents by the inquiry's lawyers.

These records showed it was "confirmed Op NORTHMOOR must end" during an RMP meeting of senior staff in September 2017, while his team were still in the process of gathering evidence.

Williams said he was "not surprised" but that criminal investigations "should never be guided by an end date" imposed on them.

The military police are supposed to be independent from the wider armed forces, but Williams was shown a briefing note by the inquiry for a meeting between senior military police officers and the deputy chief of the Army at the end of 2017, which set out the intention to close Northmoor.

He remarked he was "surprised to see it written down" but it made sense of the "pressure" he felt the investigation was under.

Williams said he still believed individuals should have been referred for prosecution based on the evidence they had found.

The inquiry also heard that the former head of the British Army, Sir Nick Carter, asked the RMP to cut the staff working on the murder probe to 25, less than a quarter of the team working on Operation Northmoor in 2016.

The police officer in charge at the time, Lt Col John McAllister, believed this would be impossible without having a detrimental effect on the investigation, according to inquiry's lead barrister.

Operation Northmoor was the largest ever murder investigation in the Royal Military Police's history but did not result in any charges.

Alan Pughsley, expert to the public inquiry, has heavily criticised the lack of resources provided to Operation Northmoor and called the decision to close it "premature and inappropriate".

The public inquiry was set up in 2022, following reporting by BBC Panorama that linked one SAS squadron to 54 suspicious deaths on a single six-month tour of Afghanistan.

Panorama found evidence suggesting that members of the SAS had executed handcuffed detainees and children.

The Independent Inquiry relating to Afghanistan is examining allegations that the SAS murdered people during detention operations in Afghanistan between 2010 and 2013, and that senior officials sought to cover up the true circumstances of the killings.

It is also examining whether the Royal Military Police's investigations into such killings were adequate.

The RMP evidence is a rare glimpse into the public inquiry's work - much of the evidence is being heard in closed-door hearings.

In January of last year, in the last public evidence sessions, the inquiry heard from its expert witness Alan Pughsley, former chief constable of Kent Police and experienced homicide investigator.

He described how the incredibly complex investigation as fundamentally poorly resourced "from start to finish", hampered by "indecision and apathy" from senior officers, as well as a lack of cooperation from UK Special Forces command.

Pughsley was clear he would not have closed the investigation, particularly at a time when major lines of inquiry were still outstanding.

articles.title: No warning before impact: Saudi Arabia’s alert system went silent amid Houthi attacks
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia stopped issuing public warnings of imminent military attacks days before deadly strikes on Riyadh airport killed at least 18 people and
articles.body: Saudi Arabia stopped issuing public warnings of imminent military attacks days before deadly strikes on Riyadh airport killed at least 18 people and wounded more than 300, as reported by Reuters.The suspension came despite a rise in Houthi attacks on the kingdom.The kingdom began sending threat alerts to mobile phones and social media accounts through a national early warning system in May. However, the alerts stopped as attacks intensified in the lead-up to last week’s airport strikes.The last public alert before the attacks was issued on September 29 for the southern province of Najran, according to posts on the Saudi civil defence authority’s X account.The authority has continued to issue warnings about adverse weather, including rain and flooding, with its latest such advisories issued on Monday. It has also warned residents against sharing images, rumours or information about missile interceptions and impact sites, in line with government regulations introduced in March.Before last week’s airport attacks, officials from an allied Western government asked Saudi authorities why the alerts had stopped, two officials with direct knowledge of the matter said. The Saudi response was that the alerts were too disruptive and that many citizens had complained about being woken up by them at night, the officials said.Western embassies issue their own alertsDespite the absence of public warnings until Monday, Riyadh had come under attack about a dozen times during the period, two Western officials said, as cited by Reuters.Western embassies in Saudi Arabia continued issuing internal missile and drone alerts to their staff, according to three people familiar with the matter and alerts reviewed by Reuters.The alerts were compiled using a combination of intelligence from the United States and other Western governments, along with information from Saudi authorities, one of the people said. They included warnings sent to embassy staff around the time of the first two airport strikes last week.However, the embassies had also received no internal warning before Saturday’s airport strike, the people familiar with the matter said, without providing an explanation.On Sunday, Saudi state television released footage of Saturday’s attack, showing travellers inside the airport terminal shortly before the missile struck.
