articles.title: The US is fighting over data centers. China is building them fast
articles.summary: Beijing aims to use AI infrastructure to play to its advantages in the race for a technology that could define the 21st century.
articles.body: The area appears like a high-tech mirage. Block after block of hulking data centers – both new and under construction – rise up seemingly out of nowhere from rolling plains and fields of sunflowers and sorghum. On their sides are some of the biggest names in Chinese tech – hardware giant Huawei, social media platform Kuaishou, service provider VNET – all packed into a zone thrumming with bustle and movement. This is Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, a Chinese city on the edge of the Gobi desert. It’s fast becoming one of the data hubs fueling a massive AI boom in China that’s made the country the only serious rival to the US’ ambitions to dominate the technology. Nearly 90 data centers are slated to be built in this city of fewer than two million people. As of last year, the US had roughly 10 times more AI data centers than China, according to Stanford University research – and vastly more computing power, other estimates show. American tech firms have something China’s don’t: access to the most advanced chips, the single most important ingredient for developing AI. But Ulanqab – with its growing number of AI and big-data centers – showcases the advantages on China’s side in the race for the technology that could define the 21st century. The towering units here were constructed at breakneck speed, with most of the densely packed Bayin Big Data Industrial Park taking shape in just two years, testament to China’s capacity to build fast. Heavy winds, beating sun and wide, open spaces give the area plentiful access to cheap green energy and land. And, crucially, throughout the Communist Party-run country, public opposition to the mass construction of data centers – the kind that is making headlines in the US – is non-existent. ‘With open arms’ At Ulanqab’s Bayin industrial park on a recent weekday, a steady stream of construction workers had their faces scanned as they filed past guards to enter building sites, while trucks rumbled along, feeding supplies to the facilities taking shape within. Outside their perimeters, vendors hawked noodles and cigarettes from makeshift stalls. The din of construction didn’t appear unwelcome to locals living nearby. Some who spoke to CNN said they were benefiting from the projects – and the influx of migrant construction workers that came with them to an area whose economy was otherwise largely reliant on agriculture. “Before, we’d just sit there and wait for customers. Now we’re constantly busy – picking up orders, doing this and that. We barely get a break,” said Ma Rong, 56, who has run a grocery store and guest house in the area for the past 30 years. “Our business has gotten much better than before,” he said. Some have been uprooted by changes sweeping the region, like restaurant owner Liu Baoping, 58, who said he had to leave his original business location due to the demolition of a highway. But he describes his daily clientele as doubling alongside the data-center buildout. “The environment isn’t as clean as before, but people’s incomes and the economy – it’s way better,” he said. Ulanqab is part of Beijing’s vision to rapidly scale up data infrastructure – a key priority for a government that sees AI as a crucial engine of growth for the country’s slowing economy with its shrinking population. “China has embraced AI with open arms,” Chinese leader Xi Jinping told a global artificial intelligence conference in Shanghai this past July. He pointed to China’s initiative to inject AI into sectors from health to home goods and hailed its push to embed AI in manufacturing as a “shining hallmark of Chinese modernization.” Already more than 700 million people use AI in China, according to official statistics. And the plan to weave AI across manufacturing, industry and daily life also requires massive amounts of compute. Beijing last month announced a $560 billion plan to rapidly scale up information infrastructure, including computing facilities, over the next five years. Private tech companies are also ramping up investment in AI infrastructure, though they still trail their Silicon Valley peers by a longshot. Such investment from listed Chinese companies will double this year to around $139 billion, according to research firm Rhodium Group. But that is still less than one-fifth of the $800 billion in AI data center investment from their US peers. And that’s not the only bottleneck. Chinese firms face another critical challenge: limits on the amount of high-end hardware available to fill these centers. Washington’s export bans restrict their access to the best AI chips, like certain models from Nvidia and AMD, while Beijing has restricted imports of some less powerful options. Domestic chipmakers are racing to catch up, but their tech still lags the US – and supplies of their cutting-edge models are tight. “If you look at the overall production cost of building a data center, chips are the most important factor, and they just don’t have enough,” said Nick Corvino, a researcher at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. But what China lacks in chips and capital, it’s trying make up for with an advantage: ample, affordable power, much of it green. Excess energy While energy-hungry data centers are straining an aging US grid that’s not expanded significantly in decades, China between 2022 and 2025 added capacity equivalent to that of industrial power sources across the entire US as of the end of 2025. And it has more green power than it can use: the country wasted enough excess green energy in the first six months of 2026 to power the entire country of Mexico for a year, findings from independent research organizations the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air and Global Energy Monitor suggest. Beijing wants data centers to sop up that excess – much of it in western, rural areas where sun, wind and land are plentiful – while boosting business for its green tech sector, under a plan known as “Eastern data, Western compute.” Under that strategy, first launched in 2022, China has designated eight national computing hubs – including several in its west – and 10 national data center clusters. Its latest five-year national economic blueprint elevated the linkage further, calling for pairing the build-out of computing infrastructure and green energy. “China’s trying to take advantage of the fact that it has this muscle memory for building energy (infrastructure) quickly,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution. “Whereas for the US, we haven’t done this kind of grid buildout in a long time and so we are struggling on the power generation and grid connection front.” Abundant power can also help China make up for its less powerful domestic chips. Chinese chip designers like Huawei are combining clusters of chips to create the computing power of superior tech. The fix can be effective for some tasks, analysts say, but uses significantly more electricity. Observers say that even with ample power, Beijing’s vision has its limits. Some computing hubs in the west are too far away to handle certain tasks at the speeds needed for urban hubs in the densely-populated east. There’s also concern about so-called “ghost data centers” or ill-conceived projects in rural areas, built to fit a topline government initiative, yet lacking the hardware or users to justify the investment. But in hubs in Inner Mongolia, where optical cables can transmit data to Beijing – some 200 miles away – faster than the blink of an eye, and top players are pouring major resources, China’s vision appears to be taking shape. ‘Get prepared’ Long one of China’s top coal producers, the wind-swept region bordering Russia and Mongolia has more recently become a hub for green energy. Fields of solar panels blanket parts of Inner Mongolia, while the slender silhouettes of wind turbines spin above grazing sheep. Along some stretches of highway unused turbine blades line the roadsides like giant, fiberglass elephant tusks. In Ulanqab, which falls within one of China’s 10 national data center clusters, nearly half the grid draws from wind and solar – and some data center providers are finding ways to rely even more heavily on clean sources. Several miles from the thrumming construction of Ulanqab’s Bayin industrial park, the Envision “Galaxy Campus” is running one such model. Spanning more than 20 football fields and slated to be among the world’s largest by area when completed, this data center will be home to servers and chips from tech companies, used to handle queries users input into AI apps in places like Beijing. Upwards of 80% of the power for the facility will come directly from wind farms operated by the company, bypassing the grid completely, Envision says. Battery systems then store wind power, while a cutting-edge solid-state transformer can rapidly adjust how much power is feeding the servers, based on demand, according to Ricky Zheng, the facility’s general manager, who showed CNN around the under-construction campus on a recent day. Water is another key resource that’s sparked backlash against data centers in America, but Zheng says it’s not an issue here. The chilly climate in Ulanqab reduces the need for cooling overall, while the facility is running a so-called “zero-water” system that uses industrial alcohol as coolant, he says. Zheng also seemed optimistic when it comes to demand from tech companies for their facilities – and those clients’ ability to kit out server racks with needed hardware. The first phase of the planned total 2GW facility was already fully booked, he said, and the company was building additional phases, both for AI and cloud services. AI chips and servers “are owned by our off-takers,” he said. “When they give us the order to build such a big data center … they were confident to have enough infrastructure to be installed in these (server) racks.” And this company, like Ulanqab itself, is planning to be ready for an expected surge in AI demand in the coming years. “We designed this for the next 10 years,” said Zheng. “You need to get prepared for the future.”

articles.title: More than 100 foreign trekkers stranded by floods in Nepal’s Gorkha region
articles.summary: Rescue operation underway after flash floods swept away home, bridges and parts of the Manaslu trekking trail.
articles.body:
More than 100 foreign trekkers have been stranded in central Nepal, according to a local official, a day after flash floods in the Gorkha district washed away bridges, hiking trails and hundreds of homes.

Bhuwan Raj Ojha, an official of the Manaslu Conservation Area Project, told the Reuters news agency on Monday that the trekkers were stranded in different areas of the popular Manaslu trekking trail because part of the route had been swept away.

“Those hikers who want to return because of the flood need to be rescued. Those who ⁠want to continue their trekking can do so from locations that are safe,” he told Reuters from Gorkha.

“There are ⁠restaurants and tea houses along the route. They are ⁠safe”.

The flash floods hit on Sunday, when a predawn landslide blocked the Budhi Gandaki River in the Gorkha district, about 100km (62 miles) west of the Nepalese capital, Kathmandu.

Authorities ⁠rescued 321 people, including 12 foreigners, on Monday, and the army said the rescue operation would continue on Tuesday, even as the water level in the river receded.

The river is a tributary of the Trishuli River, downstream from another tributary where a ‌ glacier collapse caused a catastrophic flood in August that killed 1,457 people, with thousands still missing.

There were no reports of deaths in the latest flood, but five villagers were out of contact after black muddy sludge and debris washed away more than 200 homes and damaged infrastructure, including three hydroelectric plants, national disaster authorities said.

Md Shahadat Hossain, a Bangladeshi trekker stranded in Jagat village, told the Anadolu news agency that nine Bangladeshis were waiting for a possible evacuation by helicopter.

“We have been stranded in Jagat since yesterday. A flash flood came down from above the village and flowed through its lower part,” he said.

“We are safe, but there has been no electricity since yesterday, communication with the outside world has been disrupted, and food supplies are gradually running short,” he added.

Gorkha district authorities have asked villagers living along the riverbanks downstream to evacuate.

National disaster authorities had also alerted people living along the river in the Gorkha, Tanahun, Chitwan, East Nawalparasi and West Nawalparasi districts about the flood.

articles.title: Swindon's Wyvern Theatre 'not worth spending millions on'
articles.summary: The Wyvern Theatre in Swindon is "approaching the end of its economic life", it has been claimed.
articles.body:
Spending millions of pounds on a town's "ageing" theatre, which opened in 1971, is not good value for money, a council has said.

Swindon Borough Council member Matthew Vallender said while the Wyvern had been "at the heart" of the town's culture for more than 50 years, the authority had to be "realistic" and develop the case for a modern, purpose-built theatre.

However Jim Robbins, leader of the previous Labour administration, accused the Conservatives on the council of having a lack of ambition.

Labour's plans for a new 2,000-capacity venue on site of the town's demolished bus station were announced earlier this year .

Why some have no choice but to pay costly oil prices

"Labour see the Entertainment Venue as the priority, due to its importance in demonstrating regeneration is really happening in Swindon town centre," Robbins said.

Vallender, who said the Wyvern building was "approaching the end of its economic life" said the council was now focused on securing a "long-term future for arts and entertainment" in Swindon.

"In the meantime, we will continue working with the Wyvern's operator to keep the theatre open and operating safely for as long as practicable," he added, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.

Councillor Sara Godwin said for her party, Reform, "protecting the current theatre provision" came first.

"The council should publish a clear comparison of refurbishing the Wyvern and building the proposed new venue, including construction costs, ongoing maintenance, expected income and any subsidy or borrowing required," she said.

Theatre Director at Wyvern Theatre and Swindon Arts Centre Laura James said: "We fully support and welcome the council's plans for a new venue for Swindon.

"In the meantime, the Wyvern Theatre, along with Swindon Arts Centre, continue to play an integral part in Swindon's cultural scene."

articles.title: Imran Khan’s PTI braces to fight federal takeover of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
articles.summary: Islamabad says the PTI failed to lead the fight against armed groups, but analysts question the takeover.
articles.body:
Islamabad, Pakistan — The Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party of jailed ex-Prime Minister Imran Khan is planning to legally challenge the federal government’s Sunday takeover of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, a province that the party governed.

Sheikh Waqas Akram, the PTI’s central information secretary, told Al Jazeera that the party would challenge the imposition of emergency laws — suspending civil liberties — and governor’s rule in the province in court on Tuesday. A petition had been drafted by a legal committee headed by PTI secretary general Salman Akram Raja, but Akram did not say whether it would be filed in the Supreme Court or the Federal Constitutional Court.

The federal government’s moves have emerged as Pakistan’s latest political flashpoint, with competing narratives from the government and the PTI, at a time when the party was in the middle of a delayed march towards Islamabad, aimed at pressuring authorities to release former PM Khan, who has been in incarceration for more than three years.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Monday justified the government’s moves by arguing that federal rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was needed for Pakistan to effectively combat “terrorism” in the province that shares a porous border with Afghanistan.

“No war can be won, however many resources you bring, whatever you do, until the government there leads it,” Naqvi said in Peshawar on Monday.

On Sunday, President Asif Ali Zardari imposed emergency rule and governor’s rule, suspending the PTI government in the northwestern province. The party has governed Khyber Pakhtunkhwa since 2013.

Sohail Afridi , the suspended chief minister, and some members of his cabinet have been taken into preventive custody, Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry confirmed on Monday. Afridi had been leading the march towards Islamabad seeking to free Khan, and despite the setbacks to the party, PTI leaders said the protest was still on.

“The long march has not ended. But a historic crackdown against the party has begun,” Akram said.

According to the proclamation signed on Sunday, the provincial government had “failed to demonstrate the ownership, will and intent to adequately deal with the menace of terrorism”.

“The federal government’s position is clearly described. ‘A deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism’ as communicated after cabinet meeting. That’s the constitutional premise needed for imposition of emergency,” Aasiya Riaz, joint director of the independent political think-tank the Pakistan Institute of Legislative Development and Transparency (PILDAT), told Al Jazeera.

However Hassan Abdullah Niazi, an adjunct faculty member at the Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS) and a lawyer based in Lahore, disputed that premise.

“If all of this was true then KP would be in a state of anarchy, but we know that is not the case. It had a functioning legislature and executive that commanded the confidence of the people, hence this entire exercise is an unconstitutional move against provincial autonomy,” he told Al Jazeera.

A more detailed case was set out last month in a 14-page white paper presented in Islamabad by Ikhtiar Wali Khan, a political advisor to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif from the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PMLN).

The paper pointed to rising police deaths, staff and equipment shortages in the provincial counterterrorism department, and spending priorities.

However, Akram rejected the charge that the PTI had failed to lead the fight.

He said the provincial government had paid 1.83 billion rupees ($6.6 million) from its own funds to the families of more than 900 soldiers, police and paramilitary personnel killed fighting armed groups, a contribution he said no other province had made.

Naqvi said at a news conference in Islamabad on Sunday that the federal government had been involved in negotiations with the PTI on a proposed “sit-in” by the party in support of Khan.

“We have no problem with the sit-in. Do the sit-in as eagerly as you like, we have no issue with the sit-in. Our issue is entirely terrorism-related, and we want to get you on board on that,” he said.

Taimur Jhagra, a PTI leader and former provincial finance minister, also said the talks with the government that the party had agreed to were meant to focus on Khan .

“It’s absurd that a negotiation about a protest movement to give Imran Khan Supreme Court-ordered medical and visitation rights becomes a negotiation about terrorism strategy,” he told Al Jazeera.

Naqvi also said the PTI had agreed during the talks that emergency rule should be imposed in 12 districts of the province.

Akram rejected that claim and said the party had refused. The party feared residents would bear the cost of military operations, he said.

“We said ‘No, this cannot be. You cannot do whatever you like with them. We took the votes from them. Tomorrow they will blame us: you got us killed’,” he said.

Akram said the PTI negotiators referred the federal government’s proposal to Afridi, who rejected it.

Federal Information Minister Attaullah Tarar went further at Sunday’s news conference.

“This government, which has been suspended through a constitutional option, is responsible for the deaths of thousands of citizens of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa,” he said, accusing Afridi’s PTI government of being hand in glove with the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan — an armed group known as the Pakistani Taliban — and the Afghan Taliban.

There is no known — leave alone public — evidence of any such links.

According to a government white paper, 122 police personnel were killed in the province in the first half of this year, up from 63 during the same period in 2025.

Independent trackers also point to rising violence. The Centre for Research and Security Studies (CRSS), an Islamabad-based think-tank, recorded 556 violence-linked deaths in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa between July and September, up from 475 in the previous quarter and 311 in the one before.

Balochistan was hit harder. Deaths there rose by 213 percent to 829, making it the worst-affected province , according to CRSS.

The government says it acted because the provincial administration would not lead the fight against armed groups, but analysts disagree over the takeover’s purpose.

“I would say this decision is political, administrative and security. All three elements are present in it,” Zaigham Khan, an Islamabad-based political analyst, told Al Jazeera.

Ali Arqam, a longtime observer of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, disagreed.

“This is not really about security at all. It is basically a political move that they are just dressing up as some kind of administrative necessity,” he told Al Jazeera.

Jhagra said the government believed the takeover would break the PTI, but argued that people across the country still saw Khan as their leader.

“It is trying to solve for legitimacy,” he told Al Jazeera, referring to the government.

For his part, federal law minister Azam Nazeer Tarar said at a news conference in Islamabad on Sunday that the decision was a purely constitutional step.

For the PTI, the immediate concerns are its leaders and the courts.

“There has been no contact. No one in the party has had any contact with the chief minister,” Akram said.

But the party remains widely popular — in the province and nationally.

At Monday’s meeting, Naqvi said results against “terrorism” would not come in a day. There would be ups and downs, he said, and harder times lay ahead.

But Arqam, the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa observer, said Islamabad should be judged by the same measures as the PTI government.

“You test this government by looking at the exact same hard metrics: Does security actually improve, do the basic services get better, and do the promised fiscal resources finally show up?” he said.
